summary: Project Sightline is an interactive, browser-based 3D Lunar Landing Site Navigator that shows immediately whether a spacecraft has sunlight and a clear radio link to Earth for any lunar location and date. Built on NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation data, Jet Propulsion Laboratory Horizons ephemeris, Scientific Visualization Studio imagery, and Moon Trek datasets, Sightline casts 720 horizon rays out to 300 kilometers to model true local terrain, lunar curvature, and orbital wobble. Users can evaluate all 13 Artemis III candidate regions, commercial and Apollo landing sites, or custom coordinates—stepping directly onto the surface to inspect obstructing ridges, scrub multi-day mission timelines, and get an instant GO, MARGINAL, or NO-GO verdict. At the Lunar South Pole, the Sun skims below 1.5 degrees and Earth wobbles behind mountain ridges, meaning a few kilometers or a 48-hour launch slip can cause power loss or communications blackouts. Sightline replaces fragmented tables with rapid trade-off analysis for mission planners while offering a Simple view that helps students and the public intuitively explore lunar engineering.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

We built Project Sightline to answer two simple questions for any spot on the Moon and any date: will a lander have sunlight to stay alive, and will it have a clear radio link to talk to Earth? The whole app runs directly inside a web browser with no backend server.

Under the hood, Sightline works through four steps:

1. Real Lunar Terrain: We load elevation data from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) in the Planetary Data System, using 80-meter resolution at the South Pole and 474-meter resolution across other sites.

2. Horizon Raycasting: Around whatever site you pick, our engine shoots 720 rays out to 300 kilometers—accounting for the Moon's curvature—to trace the exact skyline of mountains and crater rims surrounding the lander.

3. Sky and Orbital Tracking: We calculate real-time Sun and Earth positions alongside the Moon's rotation and natural libration wobble.

4. Power, Comms, and Verdict: Using that skyline and sky geometry, Sightline computes how much of the Sun's disk is visible, live solar power, whether Earth is in view, when sunlight and Earth contact come and go, and an instant GO, MARGINAL, or NO-GO verdict.

You can test all 13 official NASA Artemis III candidate regions (each placed on its sunniest spot), historic Apollo sites, or any custom location. We also pre-computed a 2027 South Pole sunlight map covering roughly 25,000 points so you can see where light lasts longest across the year.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Landing at the Lunar South Pole is unforgiving. The Sun never climbs higher than 1.5 degrees above the level horizon, and Earth wobbles plus or minus 7 degrees around mountain ridges. Shifting a landing spot by a few kilometers—or slipping a launch date—can leave a spacecraft in freezing darkness or cut off radio contact for days, a challenge highlighted when robotic landers IM-1 (2024) and IM-2 (2025) tipped over near the pole in difficult lighting.

Usually, checking these windows means piecing together separate orbital tables and 2D elevation charts. We designed Sightline to bridge that gap for two very different groups:

1. Mission Planners and Engineers: When a launch date slips, planners can rank all 13 Artemis III regions in seconds—for instance, seeing that on November 14, Leibnitz Beta Plateau, Malapert Massif, and Nobile Rim 1 come out GO. They can also pin site-and-date scenarios side by side, map out rover paths checked for steep slopes, sunlight, and Earth contact, and export printable mission reports in one click.

2. Students, Educators, and Everyday Learners: Space engineering shouldn't feel locked behind raw data tables. Sightline opens in a plain-language Simple view by default that answers three straightforward questions about sunlight, Earth contact, and landing safety, while Expert view is one click away whenever you want the full analysis.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE WE USED

1. 3D Rendering and Charts: Three.js (WebGL) and Canvas 2D for the interactive Moon, surface terrain, and mission timelines.

2. Codebase and Build Setup: TypeScript and Vite for a fast, browser-native app.

3. Astronomy and Orientation Math: astronomy-engine paired with International Astronomical Union (IAU) lunar orientation models and our own validation scripts.

4. Data Pipeline and Compute: A parallel Node.js pipeline running across 8 CPU cores to process LOLA elevation grids and pre-compute 25,000 South Pole points for 2027.

5. NASA Datasets and 3D Models: LRO LOLA (Planetary Data System), Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) CGI Moon Kit, Moon Trek (13 Artemis III regions), JPL Horizons, and NASA 3D Resources (Lunar Module, astronaut, LRO, and rover models).

HOW PROJECT SIGHTLINE IS CREATIVE

Instead of leaving users staring at flat top-down heatmaps, we built a Stand on Site mode that drops the camera right onto the lunar surface at a lander's camera height. You can look around the true 3D skyline, see historic hardware at Apollo sites, and check exact obstacle distances—like an alert telling you a mountain 42 kilometers away hides Earth for about 2 days.

We also built a live mission simulator driven by the same real physics. You can watch a descent, touchdown, rover drive, and fast-forwarded mission play out across three contrasting outcomes: a clean GO mission at Malapert Massif (2,510 W and 144 GB sent to Earth), a MARGINAL wait at Shackleton ridge while Earth sets behind terrain, and a NO-GO landing in darkness at the IM-2 Athena site where the battery drops below 20 percent in under a day.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

1. Polar Sun Angles and Earth Wobble: We accounted for the 1.5-degree maximum polar Sun height, the plus or minus 7-degree Earth libration loop, lunar curvature across 300-kilometer horizons, and partial blocking of the Sun's disk by ridges.

2. Lander Orientation and Relay Satellites: We accounted for spacecraft tilt—showing that leaning 70 degrees away from Earth breaks antenna reach and drops solar power from 418 to 339 W/m². We also modeled how adding a Gateway-like relay satellite high over the pole bridges terrain gaps and turns Shackleton ridge from MARGINAL into GO.

3. Real-World Scientific Validation: We tested our math against NASA's JPL Horizons system across 128 points and matched Sun and Earth positions within 0.005 degrees. Our annual sunlight calculation for Shackleton ridge came out to 88 percent, matching Mazarico et al. (2011) at 86 to 89 percent, and our sanity checks confirmed zero false positives inside permanently shadowed craters or on the lunar far side.
